evaluation.positioning_hook: A trauma expert recruited into an AI-driven CIA training program discovers the system is rewriting her memories — and the man she loves may be part of the experiment.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: intelligence ops, mind-control paranoia, and a love story under pressure. The final-act reveal that the entire program may be a constructed cycle gives it a strong hook for thriller buyers and genre audiences.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script establishes its central engine early: ARC, a neural-link training system that overlays reality and learns from the recruits. Ridley’s resistance to the prompts, plus the possibility that her life has been engineered, gives the concept a sharp, easy-to-grasp spine.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ridley is a compelling lead because her professional skill set and personal history are fused into one role, and Ian gives the story a strong emotional counterweight. The supporting ensemble is functional and distinct enough to support the plot, though the script is most alive when it stays close to Ridley’s point of view.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The ARC system, the card-based intelligence interface, and the idea of training through layered reality give the script a fresh sci-fi wrapper around espionage. The repeated cycle structure and memory overwrite reveal show confidence in a bigger, stranger architecture than a standard spy thriller.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps escalating through training, field ops, discovery, and the rooftop confrontation, with each phase revealing a deeper layer of the same conspiracy. The final stretch has real propulsion because the emotional stakes and the operational stakes converge in one live mission.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of coercive-control psychology, predictive policing, and simulated intelligence warfare feels immediately legible and fresh. The reveal that Ridley’s life may itself be a designed cycle gives the premise that rare 'of course this exists' feeling.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The CIA Farm, ARC backlot, neural patches, collection cards, and live-op architecture create a world with rules and hierarchy, not just a backdrop. The script keeps finding new uses for the same system, which makes the world feel operational rather than decorative.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends sleek techno-thriller mechanics with emotional disorientation and a steady undercurrent of surveillance dread. The script knows when to play the training like a game and when to let it feel like a psychological trap.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: What begins as a high-concept spy thriller opens into a much deeper story about memory, consent, coercion, and identity construction. The cycle reveal and the final reset suggest a larger architecture that could keep paying off well beyond the surface plot.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ridley/Ian is the central engine, and the trainee ensemble gives the story enough friction to keep scenes active. The best relationship material comes from ideological splits inside the team, though the script is still primarily driven by the lead pair.

server room, observation rooms, safe houses, barracks, commissary

technical.vfx_details: Extensive digital environment overwrites, HUD overlays, simulated city transformations, memory/cycle visualizations, and interface graphics; the action is grounded but the reality-shift language is heavily visual.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, explosions, rooftop falls, vehicle hijack, close-quarters combat, practical interface effects, and simulated-to-real transition beats.

rights_flags.detail: Senator Kerrigan is a fictional political figure, but the script also references Senator Kennedy in the epilogue and uses real institutions like CIA, DOD, Georgetown, and the VA.
Apple Watch is named in dialogue.
Uber is named in a location transition.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming or theatrical genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform or mid-budget theatrical thriller potential

cost.note: The story is mostly contained to training facilities, offices, and a handful of city exteriors, but the simulated environment transformations and action set pieces push it above a lean indie budget.

cast.note: The core cast is manageable, but the project benefits from strong adult leads and a credible ensemble of trainees, handlers, and authority figures.

location.note: The script moves through Istanbul, Georgetown, the Farm, Serbia, Paris, Yemen, and Washington D.C., though many of those can be staged through controlled builds and visual overlays.

content.note: The material includes violence, gunplay, psychological manipulation, and bioweapon stakes, but it stays within a mature thriller lane rather than explicit territory.

rights.note: The script relies on public institutions and a few named brands, with no obvious life-rights or music-clearance dependency.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ARC system is a real movie engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The card-based neural interface gives the film a repeatable visual grammar that can power both action and suspense, which is exactly the kind of device that helps a buyer see franchise or sequel potential. Genre audiences and directors who like clean rules, readable mechanics, and escalating systems will lean in fast.
strengths.evidence: The training bay, the collection cards, the HUD prompts, and the repeated 'recommended action' logic all recur across the script.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ridley is built for a star turn.
strengths.what_it_means: She’s a trauma specialist whose professional expertise collides with her own manipulated history, giving an actor a role that can play intelligence, vulnerability, and controlled fury in the same frame. Prestige-minded actresses and managers looking for a breakout genre lead will see a showcase with range and emotional authority.
strengths.evidence: Her Georgetown lecture on coercive control, her work with veterans, and her refusal to follow ARC’s prompts all define the part.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The love story is embedded in the thriller.
strengths.what_it_means: Ian and Ridley are not a decorative romance; their history is the emotional fault line that the plot keeps testing, which gives the climax real ache instead of just spectacle. Actors who want a relationship with memory, betrayal, and recognition baked into the action will respond to this immediately.
strengths.evidence: Their Columbia/Georgetown reunion, the bar scene, the rooftop recognition beat, and the final cycle reset all hinge on their bond.

strengths.what_it_means: CIA training, DOD oversight, Senate pressure, and the Farm’s internal hierarchy create a believable power structure that can support a smart, adult thriller audience. Buyers in the premium streamer and elevated genre space will like that the story feels bureaucratic, militarized, and contemporary rather than generic.
strengths.evidence: Sykes, Harrison, Dawson, the DOD official, and Senator Kerrigan all shape the program’s ecosystem.

strengths.what_it_means: The cycle structure turns the movie into a memory thriller with replay value, because the audience realizes the opening is not just a setup but part of a larger design. That kind of late reframe is catnip for buyers looking for high-concept conversation pieces that reward a second watch.
strengths.evidence: The archive footage, Cycle 3 initiation, and the final 'Human Override - Accepted' button all reframe the story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The action is character-driven, not ornamental.
strengths.what_it_means: The set pieces are built around how each character thinks — Ridley improvises, Ian executes, Egan overcommits — which makes the action feel like personality, not just choreography. Action buyers and directors who want fights to reveal psychology will see a strong lane here.
strengths.evidence: The dojo fight, the safe-house mission, the tactical house, and the embassy rooftop all express character through tactical choice.

whats_special.headline: AGENCY is a sleek, high-concept espionage thriller with a built-in visual system, a star-making female lead, and a romance that actually matters to the plot. The ARC framework gives the film a marketable hook and a repeatable language of suspense, while the cycle reveal turns the whole story into a memory-bending conspiracy with real replay value.

lead_characters.name: Ridley Cooper
lead_characters.hook: Ridley is a trauma psychologist with a soldier’s instincts and a survivor’s skepticism, the rare lead whose intellect is also her combat style. She’s smart enough to read people before they speak, guarded enough to distrust every system, and emotionally exposed in exactly the places the program wants to exploit.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Rebecca Ferguson in Dune — a role where intelligence, physicality, and emotional fracture all live in the same frame. A lead actress gets to play authority, panic, seduction, and defiance while carrying a concept-heavy thriller on her back.

lead_characters.name: Ian Walsh
lead_characters.hook: Ian is the program’s ideal operator on paper: disciplined, fast, and addicted to being right, but his need to prove himself makes him easy to steer. He’s the kind of operative who mistakes obedience for clarity until the story forces him to confront what he’s been trained to ignore.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Adam Driver in The Report or Michael B. Jordan in Without Remorse — a controlled, physical lead who has to reveal the human cost of competence. It gives a younger male actor a chance to play precision, loyalty, and moral collapse without losing charisma.

lead_characters.name: Cameron West / Dawson
lead_characters.hook: West is the smiling architect of the entire experiment, a calm authority figure whose charm is just another interface layer. He reads as mentor, handler, professor, and predator all at once, which makes him feel less like a villain than a system with a face.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the performance space of Ralph Fiennes in The Menu or Ben Mendelsohn in Bloodline — a polished, intelligent manipulator who can make control feel intimate. Character actors who can weaponize stillness and precision will chase this because the role lets them dominate scenes without raising their voice.

lead_characters.name: Matt Egan
lead_characters.hook: Egan is the legacy operator who trusts aggression, status, and instinct more than reflection. He’s competitive, cocky, and dangerous in exactly the way institutions often reward until the bill comes due.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the territory of Jesse Plemons in Game Night or Shea Whigham in any pressure-cooker ensemble — a role that lets an actor play entitlement, volatility, and eventual reckoning. It’s a strong supporting part for someone who can make arrogance entertaining before it turns alarming.

lead_characters.name: Jessie Alvarez
lead_characters.hook: Alvarez is the quiet analyst with the sharpest read in the room, the one who understands that certainty is often the least trustworthy signal. She’s observant, restrained, and emotionally legible without ever becoming soft.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded-supporting showcase that Aunjanue Ellis in King Richard or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers can make magnetic — a role built on intelligence, restraint, and the power of saying the right thing once. It gives an actor a clean, scene-stealing lane inside a larger genre machine.

lead_characters.name: Wyatt Denny
lead_characters.hook: Wyatt is the uneasy truth-teller of the group, a worst-case analyst who sees the cost before anyone else wants to name it. He’s nervous, perceptive, and useful in a way that makes him feel like the conscience of the ensemble.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role Paul Dano or Jesse Eisenberg has turned into a signature lane — anxious intelligence with real narrative utility. It gives an actor a chance to be the person who notices the danger before the room does.

lead_characters.name: Chris Williams
lead_characters.hook: Williams is the quiet cyber specialist whose silence reads as discipline until it starts to feel like distance. He’s the least performative trainee, which makes his eventual compliance with the system especially chilling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained, internal role that Lakeith Stanfield or John Boyega can make crackle with subtext — a part where stillness becomes tension. It gives an actor a chance to play intelligence that never fully announces itself.

lead_characters.name: Bill Harrison
lead_characters.hook: Harrison is the old-school trainer who believes pressure reveals truth and hesitation gets people killed. He’s institutional, blunt, and just human enough to make the program feel like a lineage rather than a machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority role that J.K. Simmons or Jeffrey Wright can make feel lived-in and dangerous — a mentor figure whose certainty carries weight. It gives a veteran actor a clean command role with moral ambiguity baked in.

lead_characters.name: Sykes
lead_characters.hook: Sykes is the operations director who speaks in orders, not feelings, and treats assets as expendable by design. He’s the face of institutional coldness, but he’s also pragmatic enough to feel real inside the machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Bryan Cranston in a procedural power role or Stephen Root in a darker register — a character who can make bureaucracy feel like menace. Actors who can play command as a form of violence will want it.

lead_characters.name: Senator Kerrigan
lead_characters.hook: Kerrigan is the polished political pressure point who gives the program a public-facing threat. He’s charismatic, skeptical, and useful as a reminder that the system is always being watched from above.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of political-supporting role that can be played with the controlled polish of Michael Stuhlbarg or Corey Stoll — a public figure whose calm carries stakes. It gives an actor a chance to embody institutional leverage without needing much screen time.

lead_characters.name: Pavel Markov
lead_characters.hook: Markov is the asset who seems like a target until the story reveals how much he understands about the game being played around him. He’s elegant, frightened, and strategically opaque, which makes him useful as both victim and pivot point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact, high-stakes supporting role that actors like Mads Mikkelsen or Mark Strong can elevate instantly — a man whose face can shift from asset to threat in one beat. It offers a sharp, memorable turn inside a thriller framework.

lead_characters.name: Dawson
lead_characters.hook: Dawson is the charming outsider who seems like a technical savior until the script reveals he’s the system’s most intimate enforcer. He’s smooth, curious, and quietly predatory, the kind of man who can make surveillance sound like care.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the performance territory of Michael Shannon in a controlled register or Matthew Rhys when he’s playing layered duplicity — a role that lets an actor weaponize calm. It’s a great part for someone who can make intelligence feel seductive and dangerous at once.

lead_characters.name: Alvarez's Female Student / Recruit
lead_characters.hook: This role functions as the audience’s emotional entry point into Ridley’s worldview, first as a vulnerable student and later as a recruit in the cycle structure. She’s a mirror more than a plot driver, but that mirror is part of the film’s design.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of dual-purpose supporting role that can give a young actor a memorable before-and-after in a prestige thriller, similar to the kind of brief but meaningful turns seen in The Handmaid’s Tale or Black Mirror. It offers a clean emotional beat and a structural echo.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to stage paranoia as a system, not just a mood.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie or elevated-genre directors with at least one feature under their belt, especially those who like clean conceptual rules, performance-forward suspense, and action that reveals psychology. This material rewards filmmakers who can balance sleek interface design, grounded emotion, and a final-act reality shift without losing clarity.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a chance to build a signature visual language around overlays, overwrites, and repeated cycles while still keeping the emotional center human. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who like contained worlds that can expand into bigger ideas without needing tentpole scale.

buyer_appeal.lane: premium streamer / elevated theatrical thriller lane
buyer_appeal.detail: The script can be packaged around one strong female lead and one strong male co-lead, with the ensemble and authority roles filled by credible character actors rather than expensive stars. The sci-fi-thriller hook, espionage setting, and memory-conspiracy reveal fit the current buyer appetite for high-concept adult genre with a clear trailer moment.

considerations.area: The cycle reveal can be sharpened even more.
considerations.detail: The archive sequence and final reset already land, but a next pass could make the transition from 'training program' to 'constructed life' feel even more inevitable by seeding one or two earlier visual tells in the Georgetown and Columbia material. That would make the final 'Cycle 3 Initiated' button hit with even more force because the audience would realize the movie has been quietly teaching them how to read the lie from the start.

considerations.area: The ensemble is strongest when it carries ideology.
considerations.detail: Ridley and Ian dominate the movie, and the trainee group works best when each recruit represents a different relationship to the system — instinct, obedience, data, aggression, doubt. One direction would be to keep foregrounding those ideological splits in the team scenes so the ensemble feels like a pressure chamber rather than a support structure.

considerations.area: The international footprint can stay elegant.
considerations.detail: The script travels to Istanbul, Paris, Yemen, Serbia, and Washington D.C., but much of that geography is already being expressed through ARC overwrites and controlled interiors. A production-minded version could preserve the global feel while collapsing some of the live-op geography into fewer practical locations and more modular backlot transformations.

considerations.area: The final rooftop choice carries the movie.
considerations.detail: The rooftop confrontation between Ridley and Ian is the emotional and commercial payoff, and the script already earns it through the Columbia memory, the bar reunion, and the live-op betrayal. A next pass could keep protecting the clarity of that choice by making sure every earlier Ridley/Ian beat is doing double duty as both romance and operational setup.

considerations.area: The ARC interface is a selling point worth protecting.
considerations.detail: The HUD, cards, and overwrite language are one of the script’s clearest differentiators, so the production version should keep those mechanics legible and consistent rather than overcomplicating them. That consistency helps the trailer, the poster, and the audience’s memory of the film all at once.
